items.text: Shipped my first feature behind a flag today. Nobody noticed. That is the point.
Most React performance problems I have debugged were not React problems. They were data fetching problems wearing a React costume.
I used to think senior meant knowing more APIs. Now I think it means knowing which problems not to solve.
Week 3 of building in public. 41 followers, 2 DMs, 1 person who actually used the thing. The 1 matters most.
Hot take: useEffect is not a lifecycle method. Stop treating it like componentDidMount with extra steps.
I rewrote our form library wrapper for the third time. Each rewrite deleted more code than it added. That is how I know it is getting better.
Forward deployed engineering is just frontend work where the customer sits next to you. I am weirdly excited about that.
The hardest bug this month was a timezone. It is always a timezone.
Spent the evening reading the React compiler RFC. My takeaway: memo everything was always a smell, not a strategy.
If your design system needs a 40 page doc to explain a button, the button is wrong.
I talk to one user every Friday. It has changed more of my roadmap than any analytics dashboard.
Shipping small is not about speed. It is about being wrong in smaller pieces.
Code review tip I wish I learned earlier: comment on the thing you would regret not saying, skip the rest.
Things I stopped doing as an SDE3: arguing about tabs, writing clever reducers, saying yes to every meeting.
My side project has 12 users. I know all of their names. I do not want to lose that when it has 1200.
Accessibility is not a feature you add at the end. It is a bug you ship at the start.
I asked a customer to share their screen for five minutes and found three bugs our tests never would.
Building in public is mostly building in silence and posting about it occasionally.
Server components made me think about where data lives again. That alone was worth the migration pain.
A good abstraction is one you can delete in an afternoon.
Today I learned that the slowest part of our app was a date formatting library imported on every page. 180 KB for a date.
The best interview question I have been asked: tell me about a time you deleted code you were proud of.
Frontend is not a junior specialty. The browser is the most hostile runtime most of us will ever ship to.
I keep a doc called things I was wrong about. It is longer than my resume.
Every time I add a loading spinner I ask if the wait is the bug.
Moving toward FDE roles means I am practicing a new skill: saying I do not know yet in front of a customer.
Two years ago I would have reached for Redux. Today I reach for the URL.
Pair programming with a designer for one afternoon fixed more UX than a quarter of tickets.
I measure a week by one question: did someone use what I shipped?
Writing tests after the bug report is fine. Writing the same bug twice is not.
Most of my good ideas come from voice memos on walks. Most of my bad ones come from late night Slack.
Stop optimizing the bundle until you have looked at the waterfall.
Users do not read. They scan, click, and leave. Design for the scan.
I deleted our custom modal and used the native dialog element. 300 lines gone, focus trapping fixed for free.
The real job of a senior frontend engineer is translating between design, product, and the browser.
Small wins this week: fixed a flaky test, mentored an intern through their first PR, slept 7 hours twice.
Unpopular opinion: most dashboards are where decisions go to be postponed.
I am done saying ship fast and break things. Ship small and notice things.
Customer calls teach you which features are load bearing. Usually not the ones on the roadmap.
If you cannot explain your state management in one sentence, you have too much of it.
Thread: what I learned migrating a 200k line React app to TypeScript strict mode.
1. Turn it on per folder, not all at once. A big bang migration dies in review.
2. Every any you leave is a promise to future you. Write a ticket for each one.
3. The migration found 14 real bugs. That alone paid for it.
